claims.text: At high temperatures, the overall wear resistance of FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings is predominantly governed by a protective oxide layer.
The protective oxide layer is largely derived from the Cr and Fe components of FeNiCrCoCu.
The oxide layer reduces friction during high-temperature wear.
The oxide layer reduces abrasive wear.
The baseline is an equimolar, nanocrystalline FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating on a conventional metal substrate.
Annealing at approximately 400 °C in an oxygen-rich environment will intentionally produce a uniform, adherent oxide scale before wear testing.
The proposed mechanism applies over approximately 300–500 °C under moderate-to-high loading in an oxidizing atmosphere.
Pre-oxidation produces a fine, continuous, and adherent Cr- and Fe-based surface scale.
The oxide scale acts as a diffusion barrier.
The oxide scale reduces direct metal-to-metal contact during wear.
Elevated temperature causes thermally activated oxidation of surface species in FeNiCrCoCu.
The oxide layer cushions the tribological contact and prevents exposure of the underlying metal.
Continuous regeneration of the oxide gives the layer self-healing behavior that sustains wear performance.
Pre-oxidized coatings will have significantly lower high-temperature wear rates than as-deposited coatings.
Pre-oxidized coatings will have significantly lower high-temperature coefficients of friction than as-deposited coatings.
Microscopy and diffraction will reveal a continuous, low-porosity oxide scale on the improved samples.
Oxide formation has a minimal role in wear at room temperature or in non-oxidizing atmospheres.
The oxide composition, phase distribution, thickness, formation kinetics, and self-healing behavior depend strongly on processing parameters and oxygen partial pressure.
Failure of pre-oxidation to produce a statistically significant reduction in wear rate and coefficient of friction is proposed to falsify the protective-oxide hypothesis.
